body.objective: Students will be able to describe rooms in my home.
body.iCan: I can describe rooms in my home.
successCriteria: I can name rooms and furniture in Spanish
I can describe my home with hay and tiene
I can describe a dream home
body.hook: Home, sweet home: "Mi casa es tu casa" is a famous Spanish expression of welcome. Today you'll learn to describe the rooms and furniture of a home.

study.title: Mi casa es tu casa
study.question: How do I describe a home in Spanish?
study.passage:
Text (read aloud, written for this lesson):
Vivo en una casa en Edmonton. Mi casa tiene dos pisos. En el primer piso, hay una sala grande, una cocina moderna y un comedor. En el segundo piso, hay tres dormitorios y dos baños. Mi dormitorio es pequeño pero bonito. Tiene una cama, un escritorio, una silla y una ventana. Detrás de la casa, hay un jardín con un árbol. ¡Mi casa es tu casa!
Grammar: hay (there is/are); tener (it has): Mi casa tiene tres dormitorios.
Furniture: la mesa (table), la silla (chair), el escritorio (desk), el armario (closet), la lámpara (lamp), el refrigerador (fridge), la estufa (stove), la ducha (shower).
Adjectives: grande, pequeño/a, moderno/a, bonito/a, cómodo/a (comfortable).
Activity: draw a floor plan of your home (real or dream) and label rooms and furniture in Spanish; describe it to a partner who draws it from your description.
study.source: Original text written for this lesson.
steps: Describe it for a partner to draw
discussion: How many bedrooms are in the house?
What's the difference between hay and tiene?
Did your partner's drawing match your home?
study.product: Draw and label a floor plan of a real or dream home, and write six sentences describing it.

body.objective: Students will be able to use estar for location.
body.iCan: I can use estar for location.
successCriteria: I can say where things and people are with prepositions of place
I can explain when to use estar instead of ser
body.hook: "¿Dónde están mis llaves?" Spanish has a second verb for "to be": estar. You use it for where things are and how people feel, and you'll use it every time you look for something.

vocabulary.definition: I am / you are / he, she, it is

study.title: ¿Dónde está?
study.question: How do I say where things are with estar?
study.passage:
Estar (written for this lesson): yo estoy, tú estás, él/ella/usted está, nosotros estamos, vosotros estáis (Spain), ellos/ellas/ustedes están.
Ser vs estar (first look): ser for identity, origin, description, time (Soy de Canadá. Son las dos.); estar for location and feelings (Estoy en la cocina. Estoy cansado.). A memory trick: "How you feel and where you are, always use estar."
Prepositions: El gato está encima de la cama. Mis zapatos están debajo de la mesa. La lámpara está al lado del sofá. (de + el = del) El perro está detrás de la puerta. La silla está entre la mesa y la ventana.
Activity: "¿Dónde está el gato?": the teacher hides a toy cat in the classroom; students ask ¿Está debajo de…? ¿Está cerca de…? Then partners describe where objects are in a picture of a messy bedroom.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Learn ser vs estar for location
discussion: Why do we use estar for location?
Why "al lado del sofá" not "de el"?
What's the trick for remembering estar?
study.product: Describe the location of eight objects in your bedroom or a picture using estar and six different prepositions.

items.answer: Estar for where; ser for origin.
How you feel and where you are, use estar.

body.objective: Students will be able to give directions.
successCriteria: I can name places in a neighbourhood
I can ask for directions politely
I can give directions using commands and direction words
body.hook: You're in Barcelona and need the nearest pharmacy. "Siga todo recto y gire a la derecha." Understanding and giving directions is a survival skill for any traveller.

vocabulary.term: a la derecha / a la izquierda
vocabulary.definition: to the right / to the left

study.title: ¿Cómo llego a…?
study.question: How do I ask for and give directions in Spanish?
study.passage:
Directions guide (written for this lesson):
Places: el parque, la biblioteca, el supermercado, el hospital, la farmacia, el banco, el cine, la parada de autobús, la estación de tren, el museo, la plaza.
Asking: Perdón, ¿dónde está la farmacia? / ¿Cómo llego a la biblioteca? / ¿Está lejos?
Giving (formal usted commands, polite with strangers): Siga todo recto. Gire a la derecha. Doble a la izquierda en la esquina. Cruce la calle. Está a dos cuadras. Está al lado del banco.
Note: in Spain people often say "todo recto"; in Mexico and much of Latin America, "derecho" or "todo derecho."
Dialogue:
Turista: Perdón, señora. ¿Dónde está el museo?
Señora: Siga todo recto dos cuadras. En la esquina, gire a la izquierda. El museo está al lado de la plaza.
Turista: ¡Muchas gracias!
Señora: De nada.
Activity: with a town map, partners take turns asking and giving directions from the station to different places; the asker traces the route.
study.source: Original dialogue and activity written for this lesson.
discussion: How do you ask for directions politely?
Why use usted commands with strangers?
What's the difference between todo recto and derecho?
Did your partner reach the right place?
study.product: Write directions from your school to three places in your neighbourhood (real or imagined) using at least five direction phrases.

examples.title: Ask
examples.explore: Ask how to get to the park.

examples.answer: Gire a la derecha en la esquina.

examples.title: Full route
examples.problem: From the station to the museum?

practice.q: How is "derecho" different in Spain and Mexico?
practice.a: In Mexico it often means straight ahead; in Spain todo recto is common.
